sense: put forward terms, a plan or a motion

terms.grammar: verb, irregular; with condiciōnem, lēgem, rogātiōnem
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.73: cum lēgem agrāriam ferret
Traupman 180, 188: lēgem ferre, propose a law; pācis condiciōnēs ferre, propose terms of peace
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: condiciōnem ferre, to proffer terms; lēgem ferre, to propose a law. A friendly suggestion is suādeō or auctor esse (see suggest).
Condiciōnem ferre, accipere, repudiāre: to make, accept, reject a proposal. Also a proposal of marriage (see propose, ask someone to marry).

evidence: Cic. Phil. 1.16: prīmum igitur ācta Caesaris servanda cēnseō
terms.comment: A senator’s word when asked his view: “I move that …”, with a gerundive or an accusative and infinitive.

terms.gloss: a bill, a law proposed to the people
a motion (in a meeting); a view put forward
evidence: Traupman 178: Quis in Crassī sententiam īvit?, Who supported Crassus’ proposal?

phrases.latin: probāta condiciō est, sed ita ut ille dē iīs oppidīs quae extrā suam prōvinciam occupāvisset praesidia dēdūceret
phrases.english: the proposal was accepted, but on condition that he withdrew his garrisons from the towns he had seized outside his province

phrases.latin: prīmum igitur ācta Caesaris servanda cēnseō
phrases.english: first, then, I move that Caesar’s acts be upheld
to make a motion about something (to put it before the senate)
